readerTitle: Ten minutes to pitch a restaurant scheduling app
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 직원 스케줄 앱 창업자, 베이커리 카페의 2호점 투자 유치) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 피치는 회사 자랑이 아니라 투자자가 속으로 묻는 두 질문, '진짜 쓰는가'와 '내 방식으로 돈이 되는가'에 답하는 일이다.
misconception: 가입자 수와 시장 규모처럼 가장 큰 숫자를 앞세우면 투자자가 감동한다.

sources.text: ENT-04-03 (How investors think), ENT-04-05 (Traction) 레슨의 개념을 적용
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 매출 계산: 38곳 × 월 $90 = 월 $3,420, 연 환산 약 $41,000. 카드에는 월 $3,420로 적었습니다.
벤처캐피털이 소수의 큰 성공으로 다수의 실패를 메운다는 설명은 일반적 원리로만 서술했습니다. 특정 수익률 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.
베이커리 사례: 단골 매출 비중 60%, 1호점 18개월 만에 흑자는 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Ten minutes to pitch a restaurant scheduling app
body: Maya built an app that lets restaurant managers plan staff shifts in minutes instead of hours. Tomorrow she gets ten minutes with a seed investor.
She has lots of numbers. Some will help her. Some will quietly hurt her. Your job is to help her choose.

image.label: Founder rehearsing a pitch at a restaurant table after closing
image.brief: 영업이 끝난 식당 테이블에서 창업자가 노트북을 펴고 피치를 연습하는 장면. 뒤로 의자를 올려 둔 테이블과 주방 불빛. 노트북 화면에는 주간 근무표 UI. 실제 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which number opens the pitch?
body: Maya can lead with one slide. Which should it be?

options.feedback: It's the biggest number, but sign-ups cost nothing to give. Without usage behind it, an experienced investor reads it as noise. This is **traction** at its weakest.

options.text: 38 restaurants pay monthly, and 34 are still paying after six months
options.feedback: Paying and staying is the strongest **traction**: customers prove the need with money and time. Small numbers, strong signal.

options.text: Restaurants everywhere struggle with scheduling. The market is huge.
options.feedback: Market size matters to investors, but every pitch claims a huge market. It says nothing about whether Maya's product works.

cards.title: Where 4,000 sign-ups really go.
body: Only about 1% of sign-ups became paying customers. But of those who paid, **89%** stayed six months. That last number is the one that says restaurants need this.

cards.title: She isn't asking "Is this good?"
body: A venture investor knows most of her bets will fail. A few very large winners have to pay for all the rest.
So she asks a sharper question: **could this one become one of the big winners?** A nice, steady business doesn't answer it, however well it runs.
Maya's pitch has to show real usage today *and* a believable path to something much larger.

image.label: Many small bets and one large winner on an investor's board
image.brief: 투자자 책상 위 보드에 작은 카드 여러 장이 흐리게 놓여 있고, 그중 한 장만 크게 솟아 있는 그림. 단순한 플랫 일러스트. 숫자나 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: "How big can this get?"
body: Halfway through, the investor asks the question. Which answer serves Maya best?

options.text: "If we win just 1% of all restaurants, we're huge."
options.feedback: It sounds modest, but it skips the hard part: how she gets there. Investors hear it often and usually discount it.

options.text: "We make $3,420 a month from 38 restaurants. Here's how we reach the next 500, then hotels and cafés with the same shift problem."
options.feedback: It starts from proven **traction** and builds up to a large outcome step by step. That matches **how investors think**: real now, big later.

options.text: "Honestly, a steady, profitable business would make me happy."
options.feedback: Honest and maybe right for Maya. But it tells a venture investor this deal can't be a big winner, so it may be the wrong investor for her.

cards.title: Strong numbers can still mislead.
body: Thirty-eight customers is a small sample. A few friendly early adopters can make retention look better than it will be at scale. Investors know this and will ask who those customers are.
Don't polish the numbers. If six months of data is all you have, say so. A careful investor will check, and a number that falls apart in due diligence costs more trust than a modest one ever would.

cards.title: Now it's a bakery café.
body: Leo's bakery café is profitable after 18 months. He's pitching a local angel investor for money to open a second location.
Which point should he lead with?

options.feedback: Followers are the café's version of free sign-ups. They show attention, not buying. Weak **traction**.

options.text: 60% of weekday sales come from regulars, and the first shop turned a profit in 18 months
options.feedback: Repeat buyers are real **traction**, and a proven profit fits **how investors think** here: an angel backing a café wants a solid return, not a moonshot.

options.text: A plan to open ten locations in five years
options.feedback: Ambition helps, but a plan alone isn't proof. Lead with what the first shop shows, then the plan.

cards.softwareNote: Same pattern as Maya's app: followers and sign-ups are cheap signals. Paying, returning customers are the expensive ones investors trust.

cards.title: Answer the questions the investor is already asking.
body: **Concepts used:** *Traction* (lead with customers who pay and stay, not the biggest number) and *How investors think* (show a path to the size of outcome this investor needs).
**Try it today:** write your three strongest numbers. Cross out any a customer could give you for free. What's left is your opening slide.
